title: Enver Hoxha
subtitle: The dictator who sealed Albania off from the world

package.intro: For four decades Enver Hoxha ruled Albania as the most isolated communist state on earth. He banned religion, forbade travel, jailed tens of thousands and covered the country in concrete bunkers against an invasion that never came. This documentary tells how he did it, and what Albanians lived through.
facts: Born 16 October 1908 in Gjirokastër, then in the Ottoman Empire
Leader of the Albanian Communist Party from the early 1940s; head of government from 1944
Broke in turn with Yugoslavia (1948), the Soviet Union (1961) and China (1978)
Declared Albania the world's first atheist state in 1967
Around 173,000 concrete bunkers were built across Albania under his rule
Albanian estimates put political executions at around 6,000, with tens of thousands imprisoned or interned
His statue in Tirana was pulled down on 20 February 1991
package.sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Albania's Institute for the Study of Communist Crimes and Consequences, the BunkArt and House of Leaves museums in Tirana, Amnesty International reports on Albania (1984), Miranda Vickers's The Albanians: A Modern History, Fred Abrahams's Modern Albania.

sections.name: Cold open

lines.title: ENVER HOXHA
lines.sub: The dictator who sealed Albania off from the world

lines: Travel through Albania today and you will see them everywhere: small concrete domes on beaches, in fields, beside roads and on mountainsides. They are bunkers, built against an invasion that never came.
Around one hundred and seventy thousand of them were built, in a country smaller than Belgium.
They were ordered by Enver Hoxha, who ruled Albania for four decades as the most isolated communist state on earth.

lines.label: political executions, by later Albanian estimates

lines: According to later Albanian estimates, around six thousand people were executed for political reasons, and tens of thousands were imprisoned or sent to labour camps and internal exile.

lines.text: A whole country behind a wall

lines: He cut his people off from the world, from religion, and from one another. This is how he did it.

sections.name: The teacher
lines: Enver Hoxha was born on the sixteenth of October 1908, in Gjirokastër, a stone-built town in the south of what was then still part of the Ottoman Empire.

lines.name: Enver Hoxha
lines.role: Son of a merchant family. Studied in France; taught French.

lines: He won a state scholarship to study in France, but lost it after neglecting his studies. He worked for a while at the Albanian consulate in Brussels. Back home, he taught French at a school in the town of Korçë.
Albania was then one of the poorest countries in Europe, ruled by a self-proclaimed king, Zog, whose government depended heavily on loans from Fascist Italy.

sections.name: War
lines: In April 1939, Mussolini's Italy invaded, and Zog fled. Hoxha, by then a communist, lost his teaching post and opened a tobacco shop in the capital, Tirana. It became a meeting place for communists.
In 1941, with help from Yugoslav communists, the Albanian Communist Party was founded. Hoxha soon became its leader.
His partisans fought the Italian and then German occupiers, and also their Albanian rivals, nationalists and royalists. By November 1944, the Germans had gone, and the communists held the country.

lines.name: Colonel General Hoxha
lines.role: Partisan commander. Head of Albania's new government.

lines: Hoxha, thirty-six years old, became head of the new government. He would never give up power.

sections.name: The terror
lines: Opponents were tried in show trials or simply shot. Landowners, clergy, nationalists and anyone linked to the old order were purged.
His secret police, the Sigurimi, built a network of informers that reached into every workplace and village. A careless joke about the leader could mean years in prison.
Political prisoners were sent to camps such as Spaç, in the northern mountains, where they mined copper and pyrite in brutal conditions.
Punishment fell on whole families. The relatives of anyone who fled or was condemned could be sent into internal exile in remote villages, sometimes for decades.

Between 1949 and 1953, Britain and the United States sent Albanian exiles into the country by sea and by parachute to start an uprising. Almost all were caught or killed. The operation had been betrayed, partly by the Soviet spy Kim Philby.

sections.name: Friends and enemies
lines: Hoxha chose powerful friends, and then dropped them. First Yugoslavia, until Tito broke with Stalin in 1948. Then the Soviet Union, until he quarrelled with Khrushchev in 1961. Then Mao's China, until 1978.

lines.text: Stalin was right; his successors betrayed communism.

lines: Hoxha revered Stalin. When Khrushchev denounced Stalin's crimes, Hoxha refused to follow, and he stayed loyal to Stalin's memory for the rest of his life.
Each break brought a purge at home. In 1949, his interior minister, Koçi Xoxe, accused of serving Yugoslavia, was executed. Over the years, ministers, generals and party leaders followed him.
In 1981, his prime minister of twenty-seven years, Mehmet Shehu, died of a gunshot wound. The regime called it suicide, then denounced him as a foreign spy. His family was imprisoned.

sections.name: War on God
lines: In 1967, Hoxha declared Albania the world's first atheist state. Every mosque and church in the country was closed. Many were demolished or turned into warehouses, cinemas and sports halls.
Priests and imams were imprisoned, and some were executed. In 1971, a Catholic priest, Shtjefën Kurti, was shot for secretly baptising a baby in a labour camp.
Private property was abolished, and ordinary Albanians could not own cars. Travel abroad was forbidden, and trying to flee was treated as treason. Many who tried were shot at the border.

sections.name: Fortress Albania
lines: The 1976 constitution banned foreign loans and investment. Albania would rely on itself alone.

lines.name: Comrade Enver
lines.role: First Secretary of the Party of Labour. The only voice in Albania.

lines: Hoxha's speeches and memoirs filled dozens of volumes, and Albanians were expected to study them. His portrait hung in every office and classroom.

Convinced that the Americans, the Soviets or Albania's neighbours would invade, he ordered bunkers built across the country, mostly in the 1970s and early 1980s. They swallowed concrete and steel that a poor country badly needed.
State media told Albanians they lived in a socialist paradise, surrounded by enemies. Some secretly tuned in to Italian television. Being reported for it could be dangerous.
Even culture was dangerous. After a song festival on state television in 1972 was judged too Western, its organisers and their political patrons were purged, and some were imprisoned.
By the 1980s, Albania was still the poorest country in Europe. Food was rationed and queues were long.

His defenders point to real changes. Literacy, once rare, became almost universal. By 1970, electricity reached every village. Women gained rights unheard of in traditional Albanian society, and the country answered to no foreign power.

sections.name: Collapse
lines: Enver Hoxha died on the eleventh of April 1985, after years of illness. He was seventy-six.
The country went into official mourning. His chosen successor, Ramiz Alia, promised continuity, and for a few years he kept the system as Hoxha had left it.
But communism was collapsing across Eastern Europe. In July 1990, thousands of Albanians climbed into foreign embassies in Tirana, desperate to leave.
In February 1991, crowds in the main square of Tirana pulled down a giant statue of Hoxha.
Tens of thousands fled to Italy on overcrowded ships from ports such as Durrës. That spring, Albania held its first multi-party elections.
His widow, Nexhmije, was convicted of misusing state funds and imprisoned. His body was dug up from the national martyrs' cemetery and reburied in an ordinary grave.

sections.name: Legacy
lines: Today Albania is a democracy and a member of NATO, and hopes to join the European Union.
Some of the bunkers have become museums. One, built for Hoxha's government, now tells the story of the Sigurimi and its victims.
Another museum fills the secret police's old surveillance headquarters, known as the House of Leaves, with the bugs, cameras and files used to spy on ordinary Albanians.

Hoxha said he was protecting Albania from its enemies. He built a fortress so complete that its own people could not get out. The bunkers were never used against an invader. They stand as monuments to the fear that kept him in power.
Many families are still searching for the remains of relatives who were executed in those years and buried in unmarked graves.
